items.stem: In a playscript, where do the character's name and lines appear?
options: Inside speech marks in a paragraph
At the end of the play
The name appears before each speech, followed by the lines
items.answer: The name appears before each speech, followed by the lines
items.markingKey: D. Playscripts do not use speech marks.

items.stem: Priya writes: "Stage directions are optional details that can be ignored." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Stage directions often carry vital meaning (a knock, a blackout, a character's tone) that changes how scenes are understood.
items.markingKey: Stage directions often carry vital meaning (a knock, a blackout, a character's tone) that changes how scenes are understood. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a playscript and a novel.
items.answer: A playscript is written to be performed, using dialogue and stage directions; a novel is written to be read, using a narrator who can describe thoughts and settings directly.
items.markingKey: A playscript is written to be performed, using dialogue and stage directions; a novel is written to be read, using a narrator who can describe thoughts and settings directly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer:

(The door creaks open.) – 1 mark for name and colon format, 1 for stage directions in brackets.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a playscript for young actors.

SCENE 2. A school hall. Night. Rain hammers on the roof. The lights flicker.
ANA: (whispering) Did you hear that?
LUCAS: It's the wind. (He doesn't look up from his phone.)
ANA: The wind doesn't knock three times.
(A knock. Three times. LUCAS slowly lowers his phone.)
LUCAS: (forcing a laugh) OK. That's... a very polite wind.
(The lights go out. Blackout.)

Outline the conventions of the text type used here, with examples from the extract.
items.answer: It is a playscript extract. Conventions: character names before speeches, dialogue, stage directions in italics or brackets, and acts and scenes. In this text, for example: "(A knock. Three times. LUCAS slowly lowers his phone.)" (stage directions) and ending the scene with a blackout, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.
items.markingKey: It is a playscript extract. Conventions: character names before speeches, dialogue, stage directions in italics or brackets, and acts and scenes. In this text, for example: "(A knock. Three times. LUCAS slowly lowers his phone.)" (stage directions) and ending the scene with a blackout, each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "A playscript is incomplete until it is performed."
items.answer: A playscript is designed for performance, so it is fully realised on stage, but careful readers can still interpret it richly on the page.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: plays are written for performance; acting and staging add meaning. Arguments against: readers can imagine the performance; scripts can be analysed as literature. Supported judgement: A playscript is designed for performance, so it is fully realised on stage, but careful readers can still interpret it richly on the page.

items.stem: Define the term "playscript".
items.answer: The written text of a play, including character names, dialogue and stage directions
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the written text of a play, including character names, dialogue and stage directions. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why stage directions are important even though the audience does not hear them.
items.answer: They shape what the audience sees and feels – movement, lighting, sound and tone of voice – so they carry meaning in performance.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a playscript about a school talent show.

Backstage. Dim light. PRIYA paces, muttering lines. JAKE sits on an amp, eating crisps.
PRIYA: What if I forget the words? What if my voice cracks? What if everyone laughs?
JAKE: (crunching) What if you're brilliant?
PRIYA: (stops pacing) That's... not helpful.
JAKE: (standing, serious for once) Priya. You sang in the lift on the way here. Three people clapped. One was the lift man.
(Offstage, a voice calls: 'Priya Shah!' PRIYA freezes. JAKE gives her a thumbs up. She walks into the light.)

How would you describe the writer's tone? Refer to two language choices that create it.
items.answer: The tone is comic and encouraging: Jake's jokes ease Priya's nerves and lead to an uplifting end.
items.markingKey: The tone is comic and encouraging: Jake's jokes ease Priya's nerves and lead to an uplifting end. items.stem:
Read the following extract from a comic playscript set in a market in Marrakech.

A busy market stall piled with lanterns. YOUSSEF (14) is minding the stall for his uncle. A TOURIST approaches, holding a map upside down.
TOURIST: (loudly, slowly) HOW. MUCH. IS. THIS?
YOUSSEF: (in perfect English) It's two hundred dirhams. Also, your map is upside down.
TOURIST: (turns the map, embarrassed) Oh! You speak English!
YOUSSEF: And French. And Arabic. And a bit of Spanish. (He grins.) For you, a special price: one hundred and ninety.
(The TOURIST laughs. UNCLE HASSAN appears behind the lanterns, shaking his head.)

Answer the following question in a well-organised response of about 250 words: How does the playwright use dialogue and stage directions to create comedy and character?
items.answer: The stage direction "(loudly, slowly)" and the full stops in "HOW. MUCH. IS. THIS?" show the tourist's assumption; the reversal "(in perfect English)" and the upside-down map overturn it. Youssef's listed languages and cheeky "special price" reveal his wit, and Uncle Hassan shaking his head adds a final visual joke.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The stage direction "(loudly, slowly)" and the full stops in "HOW. MUCH. IS. THIS?" show the tourist's assumption; the reversal "(in perfect English)" and the upside-down map overturn it. Youssef's listed languages and cheeky "special price" reveal his wit, and Uncle Hassan shaking his head adds a final visual joke. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "comic relief".
items.answer: A humorous moment that releases tension in a serious or frightening scene
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a humorous moment that releases tension in a serious or frightening scene. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Instructions in a playscript, usually in brackets or italics, about movement, setting, lighting, sound and how lines are spoken"?
items.answer: stage directions
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of stage directions.

items.stem: A student claims: "Staging choices are decoration and do not change the meaning of a scene." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Set, lighting, costume and blocking shape mood, focus and how the audience interprets characters and events.
items.markingKey: Set, lighting, costume and blocking shape mood, focus and how the audience interprets characters and events. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why playwrights rely on dialogue to reveal character.
items.answer: There is usually no narrator, so what characters say – and how – is the main way the audience learns about them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: There is usually no narrator, so what characters say – and how – is the main way the audience learns about them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a novel and a playscript.
items.answer: A playscript is written to be performed, using dialogue and stage directions; a novel is written to be read, using a narrator who can describe thoughts and settings directly.
items.markingKey: A playscript is written to be performed, using dialogue and stage directions; a novel is written to be read, using a narrator who can describe thoughts and settings directly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a playscript for young actors.

SCENE 2. A school hall. Night. Rain hammers on the roof. The lights flicker.
ANA: (whispering) Did you hear that?
LUCAS: It's the wind. (He doesn't look up from his phone.)
ANA: The wind doesn't knock three times.
(A knock. Three times. LUCAS slowly lowers his phone.)
LUCAS: (forcing a laugh) OK. That's... a very polite wind.
(The lights go out. Blackout.)

Explain how ending the scene with a blackout contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: Ending the scene with a blackout: the sudden darkness creates a cliffhanger, leaving the audience in suspense.
items.markingKey: Ending the scene with a blackout: the sudden darkness creates a cliffhanger, leaving the audience in suspense. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a playscript about a school talent show.

Backstage. Dim light. PRIYA paces, muttering lines. JAKE sits on an amp, eating crisps.
PRIYA: What if I forget the words? What if my voice cracks? What if everyone laughs?
JAKE: (crunching) What if you're brilliant?
PRIYA: (stops pacing) That's... not helpful.
JAKE: (standing, serious for once) Priya. You sang in the lift on the way here. Three people clapped. One was the lift man.
(Offstage, a voice calls: 'Priya Shah!' PRIYA freezes. JAKE gives her a thumbs up. She walks into the light.)

What impression does the reader get of the main character? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: Priya is anxious and self-doubting (repeated "What if..." questions, pacing); Jake seems careless (eating crisps on an amp) but is a loyal, funny friend who becomes "serious for once" to encourage her.
items.markingKey: Priya is anxious and self-doubting (repeated "What if..." questions, pacing); Jake seems careless (eating crisps on an amp) but is a loyal, funny friend who becomes "serious for once" to encourage her. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a comic playscript set in a market in Marrakech.

A busy market stall piled with lanterns. YOUSSEF (14) is minding the stall for his uncle. A TOURIST approaches, holding a map upside down.
TOURIST: (loudly, slowly) HOW. MUCH. IS. THIS?
YOUSSEF: (in perfect English) It's two hundred dirhams. Also, your map is upside down.
TOURIST: (turns the map, embarrassed) Oh! You speak English!
YOUSSEF: And French. And Arabic. And a bit of Spanish. (He grins.) For you, a special price: one hundred and ninety.
(The TOURIST laughs. UNCLE HASSAN appears behind the lanterns, shaking his head.)

Outline the conventions of the text type used here, with examples from the extract.
items.answer: It is a playscript extract. Conventions: character names before speeches, dialogue, stage directions in italics or brackets, and acts and scenes. In this text, for example: "And French. And Arabic. And a bit of Spanish." (listing in dialogue), each chosen to suit the purpose and audience.
items.markingKey: It is a playscript extract. Conventions: character names before speeches, dialogue, stage directions in italics or brackets, and acts and scenes. In this text, for example: "And French. And Arabic. And a bit of Spanish." (listing in dialogue), each chosen to suit the purpose and audience. items.stem: Suggest a lighting and a sound effect for a scene in which two friends say goodbye at a train station at night, and explain each.
items.answer: Any valid choices with reasons, e.g. a single cold spotlight to isolate them (loneliness); a distant train whistle to signal departure.

Read the following extract from a playscript for young actors.

SCENE 2. A school hall. Night. Rain hammers on the roof. The lights flicker.
ANA: (whispering) Did you hear that?
LUCAS: It's the wind. (He doesn't look up from his phone.)
ANA: The wind doesn't knock three times.
(A knock. Three times. LUCAS slowly lowers his phone.)
LUCAS: (forcing a laugh) OK. That's... a very polite wind.
(The lights go out. Blackout.)

How does the playwright use dialogue and stage directions to build suspense?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The opening stage directions (rain "hammers", lights "flicker") set an unsettling atmosphere. Ana's whispered question and her line "The wind doesn't knock three times" raise fear, which the stage direction immediately confirms. Lucas's forced joke ("a very polite wind") gives comic relief that ironically shows his fear, and the final blackout leaves the audience on a cliffhanger.

items.stem: "A playscript is incomplete until it is performed." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: A playscript is designed for performance, so it is fully realised on stage, but careful readers can still interpret it richly on the page.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: plays are written for performance; acting and staging add meaning. Arguments against: readers can imagine the performance; scripts can be analysed as literature.
